title: Transactions and safe updates
summary: Keep a book-copy claim and its loan record together. Use a small SQLite transaction and conditional update to prevent a second claim.
introduction: Two learners reach for the last library copy. Both saw it on the shelf a moment ago. The system needs a rule that chooses one borrower without promising the same copy twice.
learningObjectives: Explain why separate read and write steps can race
Keep related changes in one transaction
Use a conditional change to claim an available item

blocks.text: A **transaction** groups database work into one unit. **Commit** saves its changes together. **Rollback** cancels its uncommitted changes. This helps keep related facts consistent.

A **race** happens when work overlaps in a way that changes the result. If two requests both read available=true and later write a loan, both may think they won. A check made earlier is not enough by itself.
Use a database operation that changes the copy only if it is still available. Then create the loan only if that change succeeded. Put these related steps in the same transaction.

This SQLite example runs in the browser's SQL playground with fictional records. BEGIN IMMEDIATE takes a write lock for the short transaction. SQLite allows one writer at a time; other databases may use different locking rules.

items: Create one available copy, ID 203, and an empty loan table. copy_id is unique in this table of active loans.
Learner A starts a transaction and changes available from 1 to 0, but only if it was still 1.
SQLite changes() reports the number of rows changed by the immediately preceding write. Insert a loan only when that number is 1, then commit.
Learner B tries the same conditional change. It changes zero rows because the copy is already claimed, so no second loan is inserted.
Read the final state: copy 203 is unavailable and has one active borrower, Learner A.

blocks.title: Transactions and safe updates example

blocks.text: The database keeps the claim and loan together. The primary key on copy_id is a second guard against two active loans for the same copy. A real library would keep returned-loan history separately or design an equivalent active-loan rule.
The two attempts run one after the other here, so this is a small model of the rule rather than a real concurrency test. A real app must also handle waiting or busy errors when writers overlap.

If any write inside the transaction fails, the caller must roll back the transaction. Do not commit a copy claim after the loan insert fails. The success example above does not include application error handling.
Keep transactions short. Waiting for a user to answer or calling a slow external service while holding a lock can delay other work.
A database rollback cannot unsend an email that already left the system. Save the required data first, then arrange external follow-up work with a clear retry rule.
changes() is specific to this SQLite example. Other databases and drivers expose affected-row counts differently. Learn the rules of the real database before translating the pattern.

items: Reverse the two borrower names so Learner B makes the first attempt. Predict the final active borrower.
Learner B gets the copy. The second attempt still changes zero rows. The rule is about the first successful claim, not a preferred name.

blocks.title: A common mistake
blocks.text: Do not check availability in one request and create an unguarded loan later. Claim the item conditionally and keep related writes in one transaction.
